A.explanation: Superposition does not require equal amplitudes. Waves of different amplitude still add displacement by displacement to give a resultant pattern.

B.explanation: Superposition adds displacements of the same physical quantity, so both waves must be of the same type, for example both sound waves or both waves on a string.

C.explanation: Longitudinal waves such as sound also superpose to form interference and stationary wave patterns, so transverse is not required.

D.explanation: Waves travelling in the same direction also superpose to give interference. Opposite directions is only the special case for a stationary wave.

hints: Notice the word must in the question - look for a condition without which a single resultant displacement cannot even be defined.
Recall the superposition rule that resultant displacement equals the vector sum of the individual displacements at each point.
Ask whether adding a pressure variation to a transverse string displacement makes sense, and whether interference needs equal amplitude, transverse vibration, or opposite travel.
walkthrough: Identify what is given: two waves meet in the same region of space and a single resultant wave pattern is observed.
State the governing rule: at any point the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the displacements due to each wave alone, $x = x_1 + x_2$.
Explain the requirement for that sum to be meaningful: $x_1$ and $x_2$ must represent the same physical quantity in the same medium, so the waves must be of the same type.
Check the other ideas: different amplitudes still add, longitudinal sound waves also interfere, and co-directional waves from two sources also interfere.
Therefore the only condition that must hold for any superposition is that the waves are of the same type. This is option B
